title: German twisted cast-on
subtitle: A long-tail variant that twists each stitch for a firmer, more elastic edge.
excerpt: The German twisted cast-on threads the needle through the back of each thumb loop, producing a twisted first row that resists flaring. Preferred for sock cuffs and any ribbed edge under tension.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from traditional German and Scandinavian knitting practice, documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) as 'twisted thumb cast-on'. Craft Yarn Council standards for needle and weight references.

glossaryTerms.definition: A long-tail cast-on variant that inserts the needle through the back of the thumb loop, twisting each stitch. Produces a firmer, more elastic edge than the standard long-tail.

content.text: works identically to the long-tail cast-on with one change: at step 3, the needle goes through the back of the thumb loop rather than the front. This simple shift twists each stitch at its base, producing an edge that is noticeably firmer and more elastic than the standard long-tail. Under ribbing, the twisted edge grips the brim or cuff without flaring. It is the preferred cast-on for sock knitters working on fine needles in fingering-weight yarn, and for anyone who finds the long-tail edge too stretchy. Difficulty: intermediate, because the thumb position requires a little practice.
4 mm needles (or the size called for by your pattern)
Familiarity with the standard long-tail cast-on
Set up as for the long-tail cast-on. Measure the tail, make a slip knot, and hold both strands in the left hand: tail over the thumb, working yarn over the index finger.
Rotate the left thumb towards you to form the thumb loop, as in the standard long-tail.

Instead of inserting the needle upward through the front of the loop, swing the needle around and insert it downward through the back of the thumb loop. This is the key difference from the standard method.
Catch the index-finger strand and draw it back through the thumb loop, exactly as you would in the standard long-tail.
Slip the thumb loop off and snug the stitch. The base of each stitch will be crossed, forming the twist.
Repeat until you have the required number of stitches.

Sock patterns frequently call for the German twisted cast-on because a flare-free cuff matters when the piece must stretch over the heel but lie flat against the leg. It also suits any pattern with a long ribbed brim, such as a hat that must stay put without a fold-over. Scandinavian colourwork patterns and traditional Aran patterns from the early twentieth century use a near-identical twisted thumb cast-on throughout.

items.symptom: Stitches not visibly twisted at the base
items.cause: Inserting through the front of the thumb loop as in the standard long-tail
items.fix: Ensure the needle passes behind the near strand of the thumb loop and comes through from the far side. The needle tip should be pointing downward at the moment of insertion.

items.symptom: Edge is too tight to work the first row
items.cause: The twisted entry point tightens the stitch more than the standard version
items.fix: Cast on over two needles held together, then remove one. The twisted stitches will still sit correctly on the needle.

items.symptom: Stitches look identical to standard long-tail
items.cause: The thumb is not being rotated far enough before insertion
items.fix: Rotate the thumb fully forward and down so the loop is wide open at the back before inserting the needle.
